posts.title: AfCFTA at Five: What the Tariff Schedule Means for African Commodity Traders
posts.excerpt: Five years into implementation, AfCFTA's tariff schedules are reshaping intra-African commodity flows. What traders need to know about Rules of Origin, sensitive lists, and the schedule phase-in.
posts.content:
Five Years, Fifty-Four Nations, and a Patchwork of Commitments

The African Continental Free Trade Area entered into force in May 2019, and the first phase of tariff liberalisation began in January 2021. By 2026, most state parties have submitted and begun phasing in their schedules of tariff concessions — but the picture is uneven, and commodity traders who assume a seamless pan-African free trade zone are operating on a misunderstanding of the architecture.

The headline figure — 90% of tariff lines to be liberalised over ten years — obscures a material complexity: the remaining 10% sensitive products list and 3% exclusion list cover precisely the categories most relevant to African commodity trade, including crude oil, processed agricultural products, and certain mineral concentrates.

Rules of Origin: The Operational Chokepoint

For traders, the Rules of Origin (RoO) framework is the day-to-day implementation reality. AfCFTA's RoO require that goods either be wholly obtained in a state party or have undergone substantial transformation — typically defined as a change in tariff heading, a specified value-added threshold, or a combination of both.

For mineral exporters, this creates an immediate challenge. Copper cathode originating in the DRC and transiting through Tanzania qualifies for AfCFTA preferences when exported to South Africa — provided the exporter can demonstrate compliance with the Annex 2 product-specific rules and present a valid Certificate of Origin from the relevant national body.

In practice, most EXIM operators at AfriTrade report that Certificates of Origin processing adds two to five working days to documentation timelines, and that verification capacity at border posts remains inconsistent.

The Sensitive Products Backstop

Nigeria, Egypt, South Africa, and Ethiopia have placed the largest sensitive product lists, covering items where domestic industries sought protection from intra-African competition. For traders engaged in:

  • Refined petroleum products: Several West African markets maintain protection on finished fuels
  • Fertilizers and agrochemicals: Morocco and Egypt — Africa's two largest phosphate producers — have been careful about liberalisation timelines
  • Processed foods and beverages: Sugar, vegetable oils, and flour-based products frequently appear on sensitive lists

Traders should obtain the current published tariff schedule for each target market directly from the AfCFTA Secretariat portal or the respective national revenue authority before structuring a transaction.

Phase II Negotiations: Services and Investment

With goods tariff liberalisation still rolling out, AfCFTA Phase II negotiations on services, investment, competition policy, and intellectual property are advancing in parallel. For trade finance practitioners, the investment protocol — currently being finalised — has direct implications for the security of cross-border structured commodity finance arrangements.

The protocol is expected to provide a continental framework for investor-state dispute settlement, replacing the current patchwork of bilateral investment treaties. Whether this will be enforceable in practice depends on the willingness of high-FDI states to submit to supranational arbitration.

Practical Implications for AfriTrade Clients

For any trader structuring intra-African transactions in 2026, three actions are essential: verify that the destination country has deposited its instrument of ratification; obtain the product-specific Rule of Origin for the relevant HS code; and engage an accredited issuing authority for the AfCFTA Certificate of Origin early in the documentation process. Assumptions about seamless tariff-free access remain exactly that — assumptions.

posts.title: DRC Copper Output and the EV Battery Supply Chain: Who Controls the Transition?
posts.excerpt: The DRC produces over 70% of the world's cobalt and is among the top three copper producers. As EV battery demand accelerates, the structural questions around offtake, pricing, and value addition are sharper than ever.
posts.content:
The DRC's Structural Position in the Battery Metals Market

The Democratic Republic of Congo's Copperbelt — straddling the provinces of Haut-Katanga and Lualaba — is one of the most significant mineral concentrations on Earth. In 2025, the country produced approximately 3.1 million metric tonnes of copper and accounted for roughly 73% of global cobalt output. Both metals sit at the centre of the lithium-ion battery supply chain that underpins the global energy transition.

That structural position confers leverage — but converting geological advantage into durable economic benefit requires navigating a set of upstream, midstream, and downstream dynamics that have, to date, largely favoured Chinese processing and refining interests.

Offtake Architecture: Who Holds the Terms

The dominant model in DRC copper and cobalt offtake is the prepayment/streaming arrangement, under which Chinese smelters and trading companies — Glencore excepted — have provided capital to mining operations in exchange for long-term offtake at prices set against LME benchmarks with fixed discounts. This model transferred execution risk to the buyer while locking producers into below-spot pricing during the early years of EV demand growth.

The Cobalt Institute estimates that by 2025, approximately 68% of DRC cobalt production was committed under existing offtake arrangements, the majority flowing to Chinese cathode precursor (pCAM) manufacturers. The implication for spot-market traders is a structurally thin free float — price discovery increasingly happens at the margin.

Copper: LME Grade A vs. DRC Cathode Reality

DRC exports are predominantly copper cathode Grade A, meeting LME deliverable specification (99.99% purity). Key export corridors are:

  • Kolwezi – Kasumbalesa – Lusaka – Dar es Salaam: The dominant road/rail corridor for cathode destined for Asian markets
  • Kolwezi – Lobito (Angola) Atlantic Corridor: The Lobito Corridor, now benefiting from a USD 553 million rehabilitation programme, offers a shorter maritime route to European buyers and is increasingly competitive
  • Kolwezi – Beira (Mozambique): Used selectively for Southern African offtakers

Transit times on the Dar es Salaam corridor average 18–22 days by road-rail combination. Insurance and security costs on the Kasumbalesa crossing have been material operational considerations; border congestion remains a bottleneck for high-volume export programmes.

The Value Addition Imperative

The DRC government's 2022 mining code amendments and the subsequent push for in-country beneficiation have generated significant industry debate. The government has signalled an intent to restrict exports of unprocessed cobalt concentrate, requiring producers to smelt domestically. In practice, the smelting capacity in-country remains limited — Chemaf and a handful of Chinese-backed facilities notwithstanding.

For traders structuring copper cathode mandates out of the DRC, the regulatory environment in 2026 is stable for cathode (already a finished product) but carries some uncertainty for mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP) and cobalt hydroxide exports as policy positions on beneficiation evolve.

Demand Outlook and Price Sensitivity

The consensus view from Wood Mackenzie and CRU (as of late 2025) projects a structural copper deficit emerging between 2027 and 2030 as EV penetration in China, the EU, and the US accelerates and new mine supply fails to keep pace. DRC production growth is constrained by power infrastructure (the Inga III hydroelectric project remains in development), skilled labour availability, and the capital intensity of new shaft development.

For AfriTrade clients considering copper mandate arrangements, the medium-term price signal is constructive. The operational priorities are corridor selection, clear title verification, and counterparty due diligence on the Congolese side — all areas where experienced in-country representation is non-negotiable.

posts.title: East Africa's Fertilizer Import Deficit: Logistics, Pricing, and the Last-Mile Gap
posts.excerpt: Sub-Saharan Africa imports over 90% of its fertilizer requirements. In East Africa, logistics margins often double the landed cost before the product reaches the farmer. Here's what drives it — and where it can be solved.
posts.content:
The Structural Import Dependency

Sub-Saharan Africa applies roughly 17 kg of fertilizer per hectare of arable land, against a global average of 135 kg/ha and an Asian average of over 200 kg/ha. The gap is partly agronomic, partly economic — but it is principally logistical and structural. Africa imports more than 90% of its fertilizer requirements, and in East Africa, the principal import corridor flows through the Port of Mombasa.

Mombasa handles the bulk of Kenya's, Uganda's, Rwanda's, and Eastern DRC's fertilizer imports. In a typical import season (ahead of the long rains, March–May), the port processes volumes of urea, DAP (diammonium phosphate), CAN (calcium ammonium nitrate), and NPK blends from the Black Sea, the Middle East, and increasingly from Morocco (OCP Group's Granuphos and other products).

The Landed Cost Stack

Understanding why fertilizer is expensive at the farmgate in East Africa requires disaggregating the cost stack. A 50 kg bag of DAP priced at USD 580/MT FOB Morocco will typically arrive at the Kenyan farmer at the equivalent of USD 950–1,050/MT, representing a 64–81% markup over the export price. The components of that markup are:

  • Ocean freight (Morocco/Black Sea to Mombasa): USD 35–55/MT, highly volatile and correlated with global bulk shipping rates
  • Port charges, storage, and clearance at Mombasa: USD 40–65/MT, including KEPHIS inspection and KRA customs assessment
  • Inland transport (Mombasa to upcountry depot): USD 80–130/MT for destinations in the Rift Valley; higher for Western Kenya or Uganda
  • Trader margin and local distribution: USD 60–100/MT across multiple intermediary layers
  • Last-mile from agro-dealer to farm: USD 20–40/MT in accessible areas; materially higher in remote zones

The inland transport component — often underweighted in import calculations — is frequently the largest single cost driver for landlocked destinations. A consignment moving from Mombasa to Kampala via the Northern Corridor covers approximately 1,700 km; the equivalent per-MT road freight cost often exceeds the ocean freight from Europe.

The Subsidy Distortion Problem

Government fertilizer subsidies in East Africa — Kenya's NCPB procurement, Tanzania's national subsidy programme, Uganda's periodic support schemes — have historically distorted private market development. Subsidised fertilizer, when it arrives late (as it typically does, given procurement delays), displaces commercial supply and leaves importers holding inventory at the start of the planting season.

The 2022–2023 global fertilizer price spike, driven by the Russia-Ukraine conflict's impact on urea, AN, and potash supply, exposed the vulnerability of subsidy-dependent systems: governments that had not forward-contracted were unable to deliver in time for planting, and farmers who had not established commercial supply relationships had no fallback.

The Strategic Opportunity: Aggregation and Pre-Positioning

For structured fertilizer importers, the East African market presents a clear opportunity in supply aggregation and pre-positioning. Farmers and agro-dealers who can access committed volumes at transparent pre-season prices — rather than navigating the spot market in March — are willing to pay a modest premium for certainty of supply. The model requires:

  • Forward purchase agreements with Black Sea or North African producers, placed in Q4 of the preceding year
  • Vessel charter or booking well ahead of the peak season congestion window at Mombasa (January–February)
  • Bonded warehousing in Nairobi or at upcountry ICD locations (Eldoret, Kisumu) to decouple arrival from distribution
  • Formal partnerships with agro-dealer networks for structured last-mile offtake

AfriTrade's fertilizer import advisory work has consistently found that the greatest margin compression in the system occurs at the bonded warehouse and inland transport stage — and that these are also the stages where a well-capitalized importer with established logistics relationships can extract the most durable competitive advantage.

posts.title: West Africa's Cocoa Value Chain: Why Bean Exports Are a Policy Choice, Not a Constraint
posts.excerpt: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana produce 60% of the world's cocoa. Yet over 80% leaves the continent as raw beans. This is not geography — it is the result of policy decisions that African governments are now beginning to reverse.
posts.content:
The Bean Export Paradox

Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana together produce between 60% and 65% of the world's cocoa beans in a typical year. Both countries have, for decades, exported the majority of their production as unprocessed dry beans — leaving the transformation into cocoa liquor, butter, powder, and ultimately chocolate to European and North American processors and confectioners.

The per-tonne economics of this arrangement are stark. A metric tonne of Ivorian cocoa beans traded at around USD 9,500 on ICE Futures in early 2026. The same tonne, if processed to cocoa butter and powder, yields products with a combined value of approximately USD 14,000–16,000. Finished dark chocolate — if the value chain extended all the way — would represent a multiple of ten or more.

The question is not whether Africa should process more cocoa. The question is what has prevented it, and what has changed.

The Historical Structural Barriers

The persistence of raw bean exports from West Africa reflects a combination of historical policy choices, trade architecture, and market access constraints:

  • EU tariff escalation: Until recent reforms, the EU applied zero tariff to raw cocoa beans but 7.7–15% on cocoa powder and butter — a classic tariff escalation structure that penalises upstream processing in producing countries
  • Grinding infrastructure deficit: Industrial grinding requires significant capital investment and stable electricity supply — a challenge for markets where power reliability has historically been inconsistent
  • Access to pre-export finance: Processors require working capital to buy beans, process them, and then sell the derivatives — a credit gap that has limited the growth of independent Ivorian and Ghanaian processors
  • Brand and channel control: The major confectionery brands (Mondelez, Nestlé, Mars, Lindt) have historically controlled the branded end of the value chain, making the economics of African-origin finished chocolate difficult in European retail

What Is Changing

Several forces are converging in 2025–2026 to accelerate the structural shift toward in-country processing:

The Ivorian and Ghanaian government floors: The Cocoa Initiative between Accra and Abidjan established a Living Income Differential (LID) of USD 400/MT — a price floor mechanism applied to beans. While the LID has faced implementation challenges (buyers shifted sourcing mix in response), it represented a political commitment to extracting more value from the crop.

EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR): From December 2025, EU importers of cocoa (and seven other commodities) must demonstrate that their supply chains are not linked to deforestation after 31 December 2020. This compliance burden has increased the relative cost advantage of large, traceable, well-documented supply chains — which happen to be the same infrastructure that supports in-country processing.

Growing Asian demand for semi-processed products: China, Indonesia, and Vietnam have become major markets for cocoa butter and powder, and their procurement is less brand-tied than European confectionery. This opens alternative export channels for Ivorian and Ghanaian processors that circumvent European tariff structures.

The Grinding Capacity Picture

Côte d'Ivoire has actively targeted 50% local processing of cocoa production — a target it is approaching, with installed grinding capacity now estimated at 700,000–750,000 MT/year against total production of 2.2–2.4 million MT in recent seasons. Barry Callebaut, Cargill, and OLAM all operate substantial grinding facilities in Abidjan's industrial zones.

Ghana's COCOBOD has been slower to reach equivalent capacity, with local grinding at approximately 35% of production. The development of purpose-built processing zones at the Tema Industrial Area is intended to close that gap by 2028.

Trade Intelligence for Cocoa Mandates

For traders and mandate holders working the West African cocoa sector, 2026 presents a more complex market than the straightforward bean-export model of the previous decade. EUDR compliance documentation is now a deal-qualifier, not an optional add-on. Buyers are asking for plot-level GPS coordinates, deforestation-free certification, and audit trails back to the farm. Exporters who cannot provide this — regardless of bean quality — are experiencing systematic buyer reluctance.

The actionable implication: supply chain documentation, cooperative certification, and deforestation monitoring platforms are no longer sustainability annexes to a trading mandate. They are the core commercial infrastructure.
